newsitem.title: THAILAND: Siam Cement sees slow 97 earnings growth.
newsitem.headline: Siam Cement sees slow 97 earnings growth.

text.p: Thailand's largest industrial conglomerate, Siam Cement Plc, sees its earning growth in 1997 remaining slow, affected by the sluggish economy.

"Most of our products are basic goods which are tied closely to the economic growth. The slower economy will certainly affect our profit growth," the president Chumpol Nalamlieng told a news conference.
The Bank of Thailand projects gross domestic product to grow at 6.8 percent this year compared with 6.7 in 1996.
Siam Cement on Wednesday reported a 10 percent rise in its 1996 consolidated net profit to 6.79 billion baht ($261.2 million) from 6.17 billion in the previous year.
"The Siam Cement's consolidated profit came as no surprise and was in line with our projection," an analyst at Capital Nomura Securities told Reuters.
He said the sluggish performance of the group's petrochemcial, paper and steel businesses was major factor behind its slower earnings growth in 1996.
Siam Cement's shares on Wednesday closed down four baht at 712.
The group's high profitable businesses last year were electronics, vehicle parts and metal units, Chumpol said.
"The prices of pertrochemical, paper and steel had fallen sharply last year. The prices of some items declined by 30-40 percent," Chumpol said.
The government's recent move to impose anti-dumping duty on steel imports will help reduce losses of its steel units which posted a loss of more than one billion baht last year, Chumpol said.
Siam Cement group will also continue to emphasise its export sales drive, with its major oversea markets in Asia, Chumpol said.
"Our increasing production capacity prompted us to find new foreign markets. There will be excess supply as our production capacity will outpace domestic demand," Chumpol said.
Export sales in 1997 are projected to rise by 30 percent from 21.15 billion baht last year, he said.

Chumpol said the recent weakness of the baht against the dollar will have no impact on its loans in foreign currencies because the group managed its foreign loans in line with the Bank of Thailand's basket of currencies.
"As long as the central bank still uses the basket of currencies system. The fluctuation in foreign exchange will have minimal impact on the group's foreign borrowings," he said.
The baht is pegged to a basket of currencies dominated by the US dollar.

Chumpol expected the group's earnings from its core cement business to decline further from 20 percent of total revenue following the group's diversification to other businesses such as petrochemical and vehicle parts.
